stops.name: Cuzco, the navel of the world
stops.campa: In Cuzco the travelers walk on three cities at once: the Inca wall, the conquistador church built upon it, and the poor town breathing around both. Ernesto haunts the museum and the fortress of Sacsayhuamán, reads chronicles in the library, and lets the stones argue with him about empire and defeat. He writes that no other word fits the city: everything here summons what was, and accuses what is. The asthmatic Argentine on the temple steps is being conscripted, monument by monument, into the memory of the continent.
stops.quote: Cuzco: the one word that defines it exactly is evocation.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, Cuzco chapters

stops.name: Machu Picchu, the stone enigma
stops.campa: They climb to the dead city hanging between peaks and cloud, and for once the diary drops its irony. Ernesto and Alberto have the ruins nearly to themselves; they play football on the sacred plaza with a borrowed ball, drink mate against the cold, and talk half-seriously of revolution in America while the Urubamba roars far below. Machu Picchu enters him as proof: a native civilization whole, powerful, and murdered incomplete. He will write it up as an essay. The tourist comes to rest; he has come to read a verdict in stone.
stops.quote: Here is the pure expression of the most powerful indigenous civilization in the Americas, untouched by contact with the conquering armies.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Guevara, 'Machu-Picchu, enigma de piedra en América', published in Siete, Panama, December 1953

stops.name: Huancarama and the Huambo leprosarium
stops.campa: Through rain and mud, on horses requisitioned from unwilling peasants and consciences uneasy about it, the travelers ride to the leper station of Huambo above Huancarama: a poor scatter of huts where the sick live almost without medicine, attended by devotion alone. Ernesto's asthma breaks him here; he lies for days in a peasant house, injecting himself with adrenaline, feverish among the mountains. The visit is short and the lesson long: this is what leprosy looks like when the patients are Indians and the state has looked away.

stops.name: Lima, Dr. Hugo Pesce, the master
stops.campa: In Lima the travelers are taken in by Dr. Hugo Pesce, leprologist, Marxist, disciple of Mariátegui, who feeds them every evening and talks science, socialism and Peru deep into the night. At the Hospital de Guía Ernesto works with the lepers, who love him because he refuses gloves and shakes their hands; when the two leave, the patients collect money and buy them a stove. Pesce is the journey's secret professor: in his clinic the two vocations, medicine and revolution, are shown to be one discipline.
stops.quote: To Doctor Hugo Pesce: who provoked, perhaps without knowing it, a great change in my attitude toward life and society.
stops.quote_source: Handwritten dedication by Che Guevara in a copy of La guerra de guerrillas sent to Pesce, 1960

stops.name: Iquitos, down the Ucayali on La Cenepa
stops.campa: From Pucallpa they ride the river highway of the Amazon aboard the boat La Cenepa, hammocks slung among traders, soldiers and pigs, Ernesto flattened by asthma attacks and reading in the wet heat. Iquitos receives them, the rubber-boom city marooned in jungle, reachable by no road on earth, and the hospital lends them beds and insecticide while they wait for passage. Here the map runs out of lines; from Iquitos onward the only geography is the brown river itself, moving toward the leper colony that has been the journey's destination from the first day.

stops.name: San Pablo leper colony, the birthday toast
stops.campa: At the leprosarium of San Pablo, six hundred patients live on the far bank of the Amazon from their doctors. Ernesto and Alberto cross the water daily without gloves, hunt, fish, play football with the sick and treat them as men, and the colony returns to them a fierce love. On the night of the fourteenth of June, his twenty-fourth birthday, the staff throw a party, and Ernesto, pisco-warmed, stands and gives the toast the canon keeps: America is one mestizo nation from Mexico to the Strait. Days later he swims the whole width of the Amazon to the patients' side.
stops.quote: We constitute a single mestizo race with remarkable ethnographic similarities from Mexico to the Magellan Straits. And so, in an attempt to rid myself of the weight of small-minded provincialism, I propose a toast to Peru and to a United Latin America.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, 'Saint Guevara's Day', San Pablo, 14 June 1952

stops.name: The Amazon, raft Mambo-Tango
stops.campa: The patients and staff of San Pablo build the travelers a raft with a roof and a name: Mambo-Tango, Cuba's rhythm lashed to Argentina's, and the colony's boats escort them into the current with songs. For two days the raft drifts the immense brown river: fishing lines, rain, chess with the mosquitoes, the jungle sliding past like time itself. In the dark they overshoot Leticia entirely and wake in Brazilian waters, their chicken lost to the river, their dignity bartered to a fisherman to be hauled back upstream. The Amazon has stamped the passports.

stops.name: Leticia, football coaches of the Colombian Amazon
stops.campa: Stranded and centavo-less in the Colombian river port of Leticia, the two Argentines convert their nationality into a trade: any countryman of Di Stéfano must know football. Hired to train the local team, Ernesto keeps goal, asthma permitting, while Alberto drills the forwards, and the team rises gloriously in the local tournament. The town pays them in beds, meals and half-fare air tickets. It is picaresque scripture: the future comandante's first command in Colombia is a football squad in the deepest jungle.

stops.name: Bogotá, the suffocated city
stops.campa: A military cargo plane lifts them out of the jungle to Bogotá, a capital under the leaden peace of La Violencia, four years after the Bogotazo burned it. Soldiers on the corners, rifles and tear gas, the dictatorship of Laureano Gómez pressing on every conversation. Ernesto's dagger, drawn to sketch a map in the dirt, brings the police down on him; the travelers are advised urgently to love Colombia from farther away. In the letter to his mother written here he takes the country's blood pressure and finds it strangling.
stops.quote: There is more repression of individual freedom here than in any country we've been to; the police patrol the streets carrying rifles and demand your papers every few minutes... the atmosphere is tense and it seems a revolution may be brewing.
stops.quote_source: Letter from Ernesto Guevara to his mother, Bogotá, 6 July 1952

stops.name: Caracas, the parting of the two travelers
stops.campa: By bus over the Andes and down to the hot Caribbean bowl of Caracas, the journey arrives at its own ending. Alberto takes work at the leprosarium of Cabo Blanco and stays; Ernesto must return to Buenos Aires to finish medicine, one exam-year left. In the hillside barrios he walks among the poverty that ringed the oil boom, writing hard sentences. The two friends part with a promise to meet again on the road: a promise the century will keep in its own way. La Poderosa's crew is dissolved; the diarist travels on alone.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, return, and the note in the margin
stops.campa: He flies home the long way: aboard a cargo plane hauling racehorses via Miami, where a delayed engine strands him a month, hungry, in the belly of the empire itself. Back in Buenos Aires he sits the last exams in a fury of study and qualifies as doctor. But the diary closes with a prophecy set down as plain fact: the traveler who returned is not the one who left. In the famous note in the margin he declares which half of humanity he will stand with when the dividing wind blows, and offers himself for the sacrifice in advance.
stops.quote: I knew that when the great guiding spirit cleaves humanity into two antagonistic halves, I will be with the people... I feel my nostrils dilate, savoring the acrid smell of gunpowder and blood, of the enemy's death.
stops.quote_source: Ernesto Che Guevara, The Motorcycle Diaries, final chapter ('A note in the margin')

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Retiro station, the second departure
stops.campa: Doctor now, and determined never to practice quietly, Ernesto boards the Belgrano railway at Retiro with his childhood friend Calica Ferrer, second-class to Bolivia, fleeing both military service and the settled life. On the platform stand Celia and the whole clan. As the train pulls out he leans from the window and shouts the sentence the family will repeat forever, announcing not a trip but an enlistment. He does not know it, but he is leaving Argentina for good: the country will next receive him as ashes of a legend.
stops.quote: ¡Aquí va un soldado de América! — Here goes a soldier of America!
stops.quote_source: Guevara's shout from the departing train at Retiro, 7 July 1953, recorded in family memoirs (Guevara Lynch; Calica Ferrer, De Ernesto al Che)
